argument: Ortega rejects the Cartesian split between mind and world, arguing that human life is inseparably 'I and my circumstance': we exist always already immersed in, and constituted by, our physical, social, and historical circumstances, not as detached subjects merely observing them. Because no one ever has more than a limited, situated perspective on reality, Ortega defends a non-relativistic perspectivism in which perspectives differ in how developed they are, and truth is approached by combining and refining many partial viewpoints, not by declaring them all equally valid. From this follows an existentialist responsibility: since your circumstances are part of who you are, understanding and working to improve them is inseparable from understanding and improving yourself, even though doing so leaves you in an unavoidable state of disorientation with no cosmic instruction manual to consult.
keyIdeas: Ortega thinks the humble pragmatist who dismisses unsolved philosophical problems has secretly redefined 'problem' as only what's solvable by conventional methods, then declared everything else out of bounds.
Ortega agrees with Descartes's reasoning but says it stopped short: thinking doesn't just prove a separate mind exists, it proves that mind already exists in the world.

Ortega's perspectivism is non-relativistic: unlike Nietzsche's, it holds that some perspectives are more developed than others, oriented toward a truth that exists independent of any single viewpoint.
'I am I and my circumstance' means your physical, social, and historical circumstances supply the actual contents of your consciousness, making them part of who you are rather than merely external.

Because circumstance presents many possible actions rather than one prescribed one, and there is no cosmic job description to consult, responsibility for choosing falls entirely on the individual, producing an unavoidable disorientation.

terms.def: The view that all knowledge comes from a limited individual vantage point; Ortega's version holds that perspectives can still be more or less developed.
The physical, social, and historical conditions a person is immersed in, which Ortega treats as literally part of the self, not merely external.
Ortega's description of philosophy as requiring both the humility to discard one's framework and the bravery to venture toward an unproven new one.
The Cartesian assumption that mind and world are separate realms, which Ortega rejects in favor of a unified 'human reality in the world.'
